unit.title: Swift foundations
unit.summary: Seven mentor-led sessions connect Kotlin experience to Swift values, states, service contracts, ownership, build tools, deterministic tests, and evidence-based repository reading.

lessons.title: Swift bindings, optionals, and value semantics
lessons.summary: See what changes when you copy a Swift value, share an object, or leave a value missing.
objectives: Tell whether let or var lets you replace a value, change its fields, or edit a shared object.
Handle a missing value with if let, guard let, ?. or ??, and explain each choice.
Predict what assignment does to structs, classes, arrays, and objects stored inside them.
Read call labels, calculated properties, number sizes, and access rules in a real model.

sections.title: Copy a draft without changing the first one
sections.html:
Imagine editing an Android form while the saved draft stays visible behind it. In Kotlin, you may use a data class and copy(). In Swift, a value type lets each assigned draft keep its own value. First, predict what the user sees after an edit. The examples use made-up data. They run in a standalone Swift file and need no screen or app target.

Begin with three separate questions: can the variable be reassigned, can the value be mutated, and do two variables identify one shared object? Experienced developers often collapse these questions because ordinary Kotlin objects are references. Swift makes the distinction unavoidable. Prefer let when the binding should stay fixed, then introduce var only at an intentional mutation point. Neither spelling by itself means thread safety, deep immutability, or persistence.

data class Draft(var providerName: String)
val original = Draft("Dr. Ada")
val edited = original
edited.providerName = "Dr. Lin"
println(original.providerName) // Dr. Lin

The Kotlin example aliases one object. A generated data-class copy() creates a different outer instance but can preserve references to nested mutable objects. Keep that boundary in mind when reading the Swift version.

sections.title: Read names, types, and call labels
sections.html:
A binding is a name used to reach a value. Swift puts its type after a colon: let count: Int = 2. Int means a whole number. In let count = 2, Swift works out that type itself. let fixes the binding; var allows changes. Braces group declarations and steps. Semicolons are usually optional. [String] means an array of text values.

struct Draft {
    var providerName: String
    var patientName: String?
}

var original = Draft(providerName: "Dr. Ada", patientName: nil)
var edited = original
edited.providerName = "Dr. Lin"
print(original.providerName) // Dr. Ada
print(edited.providerName)   // Dr. Lin

struct declares a value type. For this simple struct, Swift supplies a memberwise initializer: a call that creates a value from its stored fields. providerName: and patientName: label those inputs. They are not map keys. Writing your own initializer can change which automatic initializer is available. Swift does not generate a Kotlin-style copy() method.

Read func title(for draft: Draft) -> String as a function called title(for:), with external label for, local parameter name draft, and a string return value. A leading underscore removes an external label: func inspect(_ draft: Draft) is called inspect(original). These small labels make large APIs readable.

sections.title: Find which edits stay separate and which are shared
sections.html:
A struct groups fields into one value. Assign it to another variable, then change the second value: the first keeps its own fields. This is called value semantics. It describes the result you can observe. It does not promise that Swift copies every byte at assignment. Arrays and dictionaries also behave as values. Swift can share their storage until an edit needs separate storage.

final class Notes {
    var text = "Initial"
}

struct SharedDraft {
    var providerName: String
    let notes: Notes
}

let first = SharedDraft(providerName: "Dr. Ada", notes: Notes())
let second = first
second.notes.text = "Shared change"
print(first.notes.text) // Shared change

final class declares an object type that cannot be subclassed. Notes has a default text value, so Notes() can create it here. Both SharedDraft values point to that one Notes object. Assigning the struct does not clone Notes. Even a let-bound struct can allow notes.text to change: the stored reference stays the same while the object it points to changes.

Conversely, first.providerName = "New" would fail because it changes a stored part of a struct bound with let. A class bound with let can still expose mutable var properties. Use === to ask whether two class references identify one instance. == asks about equality and needs suitable conformance; it is not an identity operator.

sections.title: Tell missing text from empty text
sections.html:
An optional holds either a value or nothing. String? means optional text; nil means the text is missing. A missing name, a present empty string, and the label shown as a fallback are different facts. Kotlin nullable types offer a useful starting point. Swift asks you to unwrap the optional: first check it exists, then use its contained String where ordinary text is required.

let patientName: String? = nil
let visibleName = patientName ?? "Unknown"
print(visibleName)

if let name = patientName {
    print("Present: \(name)")
} else {
    print("Name was absent")
}

let length: Int? = patientName?.count
print(length ?? 0)

?? supplies a fallback only for nil; an empty present string stays empty. if let name = patientName creates a nonoptional local constant inside the success branch, while leaving the original optional unchanged. Optional chaining with ?. skips the access when the receiver is absent and returns an optional result. It does not validate the contents of a present value.

A postfix ! forces unwrapping and traps if the value is absent. A fixture being nonnil today is not a lifetime invariant for a production field. Avoid force unwraps in these exercises: express what absence should do instead. An implicit optional check in Kotlin should never be translated by sprinkling force unwraps through Swift code.

sections.title: Check what you need before going on
sections.html:
A guard checks a condition needed by the rest of a function. If it fails, that branch must leave the current scope, often with return or throw. guard let checks that an optional contains a value and gives that value a name for the remaining steps. if let gives you the name only inside its successful branch. The shorthand guard let value else reuses the optional name.

func greeting(for patientName: String?) -> String {
    guard let name = patientName else {
        return "Hello"
    }
    return "Hello, \(name)"
}
print(greeting(for: "Sam"))
print(greeting(for: nil))

Swift's Int has platform-dependent width and is 64 bits on the relevant modern Apple platforms. Kotlin Long is always a signed 64-bit integer, so Int64? is a clearer translation when the width is part of a data contract. Numeric conversions are explicit; optional conversion also requires handling absence. A sensible local count can remain Int.

A grapheme cluster is a group of text units treated as one character. Swift String.count counts extended grapheme clusters. Kotlin String.length counts UTF-16 code units. An accented letter or emoji can therefore have different counts. For a network length limit, use the representation the API specifies. Hashable lets a value be used by hashed collections and includes equality support. It does not create object identity or guarantee a permanent ID.

sections.title: Read the real question model
sections.html:
A model holds the facts a feature uses. Open CancelAppointmentQuestionData at the repository link. public struct at line 8 declares a value type that other modules can name. Its fields use let. The subtitle: String? field at line 11 may be missing. options is an array of another named type. Check the screen that reads subtitle before deciding whether missing and blank text should look alike.

The asNavigationState block at line 15 is a computed property. It returns a value when accessed; it is not an additional stored field. .question(self) constructs an enum case carrying the current model, which we will unpack next. Being computed does not automatically mean cached, expensive, or safe to repeat with arbitrary side effects.

Notice a visibility boundary: the type is public, but fields without access modifiers are internal to its module. A public struct does not automatically export all its members or its synthesized memberwise initializer. That matters when you later move models across targets. The cancellation source directory is explicitly included by its co-located Project.swift and matches the target in Package.swift. This is an active source anchor, not a similarly named file in the older tree.

Before the exercise, say aloud what assigning this model preserves, what cannot be directly mutated, and which nested types you would inspect before claiming deep immutability. That last question is a professional habit, not a trick.

quiz.question: A let-bound Swift struct contains a let property pointing to a class with a var text property. What can still change?
options: Nothing; let recursively freezes the entire graph.
The class object's text, while the struct's stored reference stays fixed.
The struct's stored reference can be replaced freely.
quiz.explanation: let prevents mutation of the bound struct value. Mutating a class reached through its stored reference does not replace that reference, so both struct copies can observe the same class mutation.

quiz.question: For a present empty string, what does name ?? "Unknown" produce?
options: Unknown
nil
The empty string
quiz.explanation: Nil coalescing tests absence, not emptiness. Treating empty as missing requires a separate product rule and an explicit content check.

quiz.question: Why use Int64? for a direct translation of a Kotlin Long? identifier?
options: It preserves the explicitly signed 64-bit contract.
Swift Int is always 32 bits.
Optional identifiers must use Int64.
quiz.explanation: Int64 states the width independent of platform. Int is convenient and 64 bits on this Apple environment, but its definition is platform-dependent; optionality imposes no special integer width.

quiz.question: What is the call syntax for func title(for draft: Draft) -> String?
options: title(draft: original)
title(for: original)
title(original)
quiz.explanation: for is the external argument label. draft is the parameter's local name inside the body. Only an underscore would remove the external label.

exercise.brief: Build a small Swift selection draft in a separate file. Show which edits stay separate and how missing IDs are handled.
steps: Declare Selection with var specialtyID: Int64? and var procedureID: Int64?. Give both a nil default. Explain each part of the declarations.
Set original.specialtyID to 10. Assign original to edited. Change only edited.specialtyID to 20.
Print both specialties with ??. Use if let for a present ID. Use guard let in a function that needs a procedure ID.
Predict whether changing a let-bound Selection compiles. Explain what Kotlin assignment of a mutable data class would share.
In a separate experiment, store one mutable class object inside the struct. Show which object both copies still share.
acceptance: Original retains 10 and edited contains 20.
Missing procedure follows an explicit return path without force unwrapping.
You distinguish a mutable binding, a value mutation, and shared reference identity.
The experiment is separate from production files; attempting the work, not reading this answer, establishes completion.
exercise.solution:
Write your predictions before reading this answer. The program below runs in one standalone Swift file. It imports no client code. A default is the value used when you leave an argument out. Here that makes procedureID stay nil. Assigning the draft gives the edited copy its own outer fields.

struct Selection {
    var specialtyID: Int64? = nil
    var procedureID: Int64? = nil
}

let original = Selection(specialtyID: 10)
var edited = original
edited.specialtyID = 20
print(original.specialtyID ?? -1) // 10
print(edited.specialtyID ?? -1)   // 20

if let specialty = edited.specialtyID {
    print("Present specialty: \(specialty)")
}

func procedureText(for selection: Selection) -> String {
    guard let procedure = selection.procedureID else {
        return "No procedure selected"
    }
    return "Procedure \(procedure)"
}
print(procedureText(for: edited))

The -1 is an output-only teaching fallback, not a stored sentinel or valid identifier. Keeping nil in the model preserves the domain fact that no procedure was selected. The local specialty binding is nonoptional only within its branch; the procedure binding remains usable after the guard.

Changing original.specialtyID fails because original is a let-bound struct. Kotlin assignment of a mutable data-class instance instead aliases the same object. For the nested-reference extension, reuse Notes from the lesson: assign the containing struct and mutate edited.notes.text. Explain the shared Notes instance explicitly rather than claiming that all struct assignments recursively clone everything. The preserved instructor example remains a reference; your own translation and explanation still need to be attempted.

lessons.title: Swift enums and Kotlin sealed states
lessons.summary: Give each screen situation a name, carry the data it needs, and handle every possible case.
objectives: Turn a Kotlin sealed hierarchy into a Swift enum with data in its cases.
Create a case, pull its data out, and write a switch that covers every case.
Tell data supplied for one case instance from a fixed raw code shared by that case.
Keep no matches, no result yet, and failed work as different situations.

sections.title: Give each valid situation one name
sections.html:
A state says what is true now. Think of an Android search screen with a loading flag, a nullable result, and nullable error text. All three can be set by mistake. A Kotlin sealed hierarchy helps prevent that. A Swift enum also lists named choices, called cases. A single enum value is one case at a time. Start with the valid screen situations instead of copying every old flag.

A state is a description of what is true now; an action is an event asking something to happen. Both can use enums, but they answer different questions. .loading describes a current state, while .retry describes an intent. Keeping the distinction helps when you later reason about navigation and UI updates. Today we use pure Swift descriptions without starting requests or rendering a screen.

sealed interface SearchState {
    data object Idle : SearchState
    data object Loading : SearchState
    data class Loaded(val providers: List<String>) : SearchState
    data class Failed(val message: String) : SearchState
}

This Kotlin example is a conceptual counterpart, not code shared between the clients. Swift enum cases are variants of one type rather than subclasses. Swift enums have value semantics, although a class stored in a payload can still be shared, just as in session 001.

sections.title: Put the right data in each case
sections.html:
An associated value is data you put into an enum case when you create that value. The loaded case needs a list of names. The failed case needs a message. Idle and loading need neither. The declaration says which data each case accepts. Swift therefore rejects a loaded case with no array, or a failure carrying an integer where text is required.

enum SearchState: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loading
    case loaded(providers: [String])
    case failed(message: String)
}

let start: SearchState = .idle
let result = SearchState.loaded(providers: ["Dr. Ada"])
let empty: SearchState = .loaded(providers: [])
let failure: SearchState = .failed(message: "Retry when connected")

case introduces a variant. providers: is an argument label at construction; [String] is its array type. A leading dot means Swift can infer the enclosing enum type from context. The explicit SearchState.loaded spelling provides that context itself. You will encounter both forms in production code.

: Equatable asks the type to support value equality. Swift can generate that comparison here because the strings and arrays already support equality. A custom payload without Equatable needs suitable conformance or a comparison you write yourself. Generated Hashable has similar requirements and includes Equatable. Hashing helps collections find values. It does not give an enum object identity.

sections.title: Match a case and read its data
sections.html:
A pattern describes the shape you want to match. Swift switch checks which enum case you have. A matching branch can give the case data local names. Kotlin when often works by recognizing a sealed subtype. Here Swift extracts data from a case instead. Your local names can differ from the argument labels used to create the case.

func title(for state: SearchState) -> String {
    switch state {
    case .idle:
        return "Start a search"
    case .loading:
        return "Loading"
    case let .loaded(names):
        return names.isEmpty ? "No matches" : "\(names.count) providers"
    case let .failed(message):
        return "Error: \(message)"
    }
}

if case let .loaded(names) = result {
    print(names.joined(separator: ", "))
}

case let .loaded(names) makes names an immutable array binding in that branch. case .loaded(let names) is an equivalent spelling. if case asks whether one pattern matches without requiring every other case to have a branch. It is useful for optional behavior; a renderer deciding all states generally benefits from a full switch.

The conditional expression condition ? first : second chooses one result, similar to a Kotlin expression-form if. Swift switch branches do not fall through automatically, so no break is necessary after each return. Avoid importing Java switch habits. An enum's payload is not a mutable field common to every case: to change state, assign a new case or construct a new payload.

sections.title: Let the compiler find a missing choice
sections.html:
An exhaustive switch handles every possible case. For the enum declared here, Swift requires every case or a catch-all branch. Try adding case offline. The compiler will point out that title needs another branch. This is useful: it shows where a new screen choice needs a decision. Adding default too early can hide that decision behind an unsuitable old label.

Give a new known case its own branch when it needs different behavior. A catch-all should group cases only when that is intentional. An imported nonfrozen enum is one whose library may add cases under its evolution rules. @unknown default handles future cases while warning if you missed a known case. That library boundary is different from hiding a case in the local state model you control.

Exhaustiveness checks possible values, not valid transitions. The enum still permits a direct change from idle to failed, or one loaded list being replaced by another. A transition function or feature owner must define when such changes are allowed. This separation will matter in later architecture sessions: good state representation reduces invalid combinations, but it does not by itself orchestrate asynchronous work.

Likewise, avoid claiming that an enum eliminates every invalid payload. A failed message can be blank unless you validate it. Loaded strings can contain duplicates. Use the type system for structural constraints, then test the remaining domain rules explicitly.

sections.title: Use a fixed code for a fixed choice
sections.html:
A raw value is a fixed code attached to an enum case. Every scheduleConflict has the same raw string. This fits a closed list of known server codes or stored keys. An associated value is different: each failed request may carry a different message. Ask whether you need a fixed identifier for the choice, or changing data for this particular value.

enum ReasonCode: String {
    case scheduleConflict = "schedule_conflict"
    case other = "other"
}

let known = ReasonCode(rawValue: "schedule_conflict")
let unknown = ReasonCode(rawValue: "server_added_reason")
print(known == .scheduleConflict) // true
print(unknown == nil)            // true
print(ReasonCode.other.rawValue) // other

ReasonCode(rawValue:) is a failable initializer returning an optional because a supplied string may not match a known case. Decide explicitly what unknown input means: reject it, show a generic fallback, or preserve the original value elsewhere for forward compatibility. Force unwrapping turns a server adding a new reason into a crash.

One raw-value enum cannot also declare associated-value cases. To combine a fixed code with changing details, put them in a struct, or use an associated-value enum with a calculated code property. Codable is a separate promise about encoding and decoding; strings alone do not give it to the type. CaseIterable can list suitable cases. Swift cannot automatically list every possible case value when its data can vary without a finite limit.

sections.title: Keep no matches separate from failure
sections.html:
An empty result means the work succeeded but found nothing. .loaded(providers: []) says exactly that. .idle says no search result is being shown because work has not begun. .failed(message:) says the work failed. These choices need different next steps: start a search, change a query, or retry. Turning all three into an empty array loses that meaning.

An optional SearchState? introduces another state: no SearchState value at all. Add it only if the owner genuinely has no state yet. When idle already expresses the initial situation, optionality may add needless branches and ambiguity. Ask what the user would see for nil versus idle before introducing both.

Open the active cancellation coordinator. Its NavigationState at line 177 contains question with CancelAppointmentQuestionData and bookingPrompt without payload. The switch at line 53 extracts questionData only in the question branch. The separate CancellationReason at line 8 uses String raw values for API identifiers. These files demonstrate the two enum forms in one feature, not two interchangeable implementation styles.

Trace the model's computed asNavigationState from the previous session: it wraps the model in question rather than converting it into a string. That preserves typed information until the consumer needs it. Inspecting this small chain is enough today; the UIKit superclass and navigation architecture will be introduced later.

quiz.question: What distinguishes an associated value from a raw value?
options: Both are supplied dynamically at every construction.
Associated values vary per instance; raw values are fixed per case.
Raw values are class references while associated values are always integers.
quiz.explanation: loaded(providers:) can hold a different array on every construction. ReasonCode.other always maps to its declared raw string. The two models solve different data needs.

quiz.question: A new local SearchState.offline case is added to an enum consumed by an exhaustive switch. What happens?
options: The switch automatically uses failed.
The compiler requires handling the added case.
Existing branches run in declaration order until one succeeds.
quiz.explanation: An exhaustive local switch must account for every case. Adding default earlier would have hidden this decision; Swift does not invent an offline presentation.

quiz.question: Why preserve loaded([]) separately from idle?
options: An empty Swift array cannot be constructed.
It distinguishes completed success with no matches from a search that has not begun.
Enums require every case to hold a unique nonempty payload.
quiz.explanation: The distinction supports different user guidance and analytics. Payload shape and product state are separate; an empty list is a valid successful result.

quiz.question: What does ReasonCode(rawValue: "new_server_code") return if the code is unknown?
options: A new case created at runtime.
The first declared case.
nil
quiz.explanation: The raw-value initializer is failable. Unknown external identifiers need an explicit compatibility decision; an enum's cases are not extended dynamically.

Print a title for each of the four cases. Also print the title for loaded with an empty array.

exercise.solution:
A renderer turns a state into something the user can read. The lesson's title function is one worked renderer. Put these calls after SearchState and title in the same standalone file. Predict the printed lines first, then compare them with the answer.

let samples: [SearchState] = [
    .idle,
    .loading,
    .loaded(providers: ["Dr. Ada"]),
    .loaded(providers: []),
    .failed(message: "Retry when connected")
]
for sample in samples {
    print(title(for: sample))
}

The expected lines are Start a search, Loading, 1 providers, No matches, and Error: Retry when connected. The teaching string intentionally leaves pluralization simple; real localized UI would address that separately. Empty success never takes the failure branch.

After adding offline, extend the switch with case .offline: return "Offline: retry later". A separate case is justified if it drives a distinct affordance, such as retaining stale content or displaying a connection explanation. If all failures share the same behavior, a typed failure payload can be enough instead. Neither decision is universally correct; make the user-facing rule explicit.

The compiler protects coverage, but it cannot decide whether a retry should be enabled or whether cached names should remain visible. Those are transition and presentation requirements. For a raw code, preserve nil from unknown input until the boundary deliberately maps it to a fallback. Record the added branch and product rationale as your exercise evidence rather than treating this solution as completion.

lessons.title: Protocols, extensions, closures, and errors
lessons.summary: Set a clear service promise, swap in a fake, and keep failures useful to the caller.
objectives: Declare a protocol and replace a real service with a fake whose result you control.
Explain required methods, defaults, and how Swift picks an extension-only helper.
Read closure types, trailing closures, any values, and callbacks marked @escaping.
Keep success with data, success with no data, and failure separate.

sections.title: Give a service a clear promise
sections.html:
A protocol lists what a type must provide. On Android, an interface lets a ViewModel call a service without depending on Retrofit itself. A fake can provide a known response for a test. Swift protocols offer that same useful boundary for structs, classes, and enums. The details differ from Kotlin interfaces, so check the Swift promise instead of assuming the two features are identical.

This made-up service returns provider names before the call finishes. That is synchronous work. It keeps substitution and error handling visible without adding waiting. throws permits failure; it does not start background work. A later async throws requirement could also suspend. Waiting, object ownership, and execution rules are separate questions. A type being called a service is not a reason by itself to add async.

protocol ProviderServing {
    func providers() throws -> [String]
}

enum ProviderError: Error {
    case offline
}

struct FakeProviderService: ProviderServing {
    let isOffline: Bool

    func providers() throws -> [String] {
        if isOffline {
            throw ProviderError.offline
        }
        return ["Dr. Ada", "Dr. Lin"]
    }
}

The colon after the struct name declares conformance, and the colon after ProviderError makes the enum usable as an Error. Every conforming service must satisfy the required callable shape. This entire declaration block is standalone Swift and needs no networking package.

sections.title: Read every part of the method promise
sections.html:
A requirement is an operation or property a protocol promises to callers. Read func providers() throws -> [String] as: call providers with no inputs; get an array of text, or a thrown error. The name, input labels, types, and effects all matter. A fake named fetchProviders does not meet this promise. An async implementation cannot fill a requirement that promises a synchronous call.

Swift checks an effect: something a call is allowed to do beyond producing its ordinary result, such as throwing or suspending. Kotlin generally allows exceptions without declaring throws. Java checked exceptions name particular exception classes. Swift's ordinary throws needs try at the call but does not list Java-style error classes. Newer Swift also supports typed throws for suitable APIs. This lesson and the inspected service use ordinary throws deliberately.

A property requirement such as var name: String { get } promises readable access, not a specific storage strategy. A stored let property or computed property can satisfy it. A get/set requirement needs writable behavior. For a value-type requirement that mutates its own stored state, mutating must be part of the contract; that does not arise in our read-only service.

any ProviderServing is an existential: a value accessed through the protocol while its concrete conforming type is hidden. It enables substitution here. A generic parameter constrained to ProviderServing preserves the concrete type for the generic implementation. Neither choice proves reference semantics; the wrapped service may still be a struct.

sections.title: Add a helper and see which method is called
sections.html:
An extension adds behavior to a type or protocol already declared. It can add methods, calculated properties, and promises that the type follows another protocol. It cannot add stored instance fields. Our helper reads the service's names and turns them into uppercase text. It still throws if the service fails, so callers keep the chance to handle that failure.

extension ProviderServing {
    func displayNames() throws -> [String] {
        try providers().map { name in name.uppercased() }
    }
}

map calls the closure once for each element and constructs an output array. name in separates the parameter declaration from the body. With a single expression, an explicit return is unnecessary. The initial try accounts for the potentially throwing providers call; uppercasing itself is not a network operation.

Dispatch means how Swift chooses which implementation to call. A declared protocol requirement can select the conformer's implementation through a protocol value, with an extension providing a default. A method found only in the extension is a helper, not such a requirement. A concrete value may call its same-named method while a protocol value calls the extension helper. The next example prints both choices.

protocol BadgeNaming {}
extension BadgeNaming {
    func badge() -> String { "default" }
}
struct FeaturedBadge: BadgeNaming {
    func badge() -> String { "featured" }
}
let concreteBadge = FeaturedBadge()
let abstractBadge: any BadgeNaming = concreteBadge
print(concreteBadge.badge()) // featured
print(abstractBadge.badge()) // default

If badge must vary polymorphically, declare it as a requirement in BadgeNaming and optionally supply its default in the extension. Kotlin extension functions are also selected statically, but Kotlin extensions cannot retroactively make a class implement an interface. Use the analogy to ask questions, not to skip checking Swift's contract.

sections.title: Pass a piece of work as a value
sections.html:
A closure is a piece of callable work that can be passed as a value. ([String]) -> Void says it takes one array of text and returns no useful result. Void is the empty tuple, roughly the role of Kotlin Unit. Parentheses group the inputs; the arrow points to the result type. This type says nothing about which queue runs the work.

func showProviders(
    service: any ProviderServing,
    onNames: ([String]) -> Void
) {
    do {
        let names = try service.displayNames()
        onNames(names)
    } catch ProviderError.offline {
        print("Offline: retry when connected")
    } catch {
        print("Unexpected failure")
    }
}

showProviders(service: FakeProviderService(isOffline: false)) { names in
    print(names.joined(separator: ", "))
}

The closure after the closing parenthesis is trailing-closure syntax for the final onNames argument. names receives the array; it is not fetched from an outer variable. Shorthand $0 can replace the first parameter, but explicit names teach intent more clearly.

A plain closure parameter is nonescaping by default: its use stays within the receiving call. To save it, return it, or arrange a later call, declare that parameter @escaping. Put the annotation on the parameter, not on the stored property's function type. Escaping says the callback may outlive this call. It does not say the callback runs in the background, captures weakly, or will run at all. Optional closure parameters have different type rules; this rule is for the plain form shown here.

sections.title: Choose what happens when a call fails
sections.html:
A thrown error leaves the normal success path and gives the caller a failure value. try marks a call that may do this. It does not repair the failure. Handle it nearby with do and catch, or let a function declared throws pass it outward. A catch for ProviderError.offline handles that case. A final catch can receive other thrown errors as error.

try? replaces a thrown error with nil and loses its cause. That fits a rule where failure truly means optional absence. For this screen, (try? service.providers()) ?? [] makes offline look like a successful search with zero names. The caller can no longer choose retry from that result. Keep the separate outcomes from lesson 002 when the failure cause changes what the user should do.

try! traps when the operation throws. It is not a faster catch or a user-facing recovery strategy. Swift error handling also does not catch every crash: force-unwrapping nil and triggering precondition failures are not ordinary thrown errors. Define failure semantics before selecting an operator.

defer schedules cleanup as a scope is left, including after return or throw. It is useful for paired resource operations, but it cannot transform an error into success. In our simple synchronous service there is no resource requiring deferred cleanup. Avoid decorative language features; each one should solve a visible requirement.

sections.title: Read a real service and saved callback
sections.html:
A service contract states what a caller may ask a service to do. Open GooglePlaceDetailsServing at line 12. Its public protocol also requires Sendable, a promise about safe transfer in Swift concurrency. We study that promise later; it is not another word for immutable. fetchDetails is async throws: it may wait and may fail. Read its placeId label and result type separately.

The DIResolver extension at line 18 adds a lookup helper to an existing type. It calls a required resolver operation rather than storing a service itself. #file and #line provide diagnostic defaults; callers normally do not supply them. The return is spelled with a bare protocol name in this source. Our teaching code uses explicit any; do not infer a repository-wide migration from that stylistic difference.

In the cancellation coordinator, the onSubmitResponse property at line 19 stores an async throwing closure. Its initializer marks that parameter escaping at line 28 and assigns it at line 36. The later invocation uses try await. Read the callback lifetime first; execution and cancellation will have their own sessions.

The standalone fake proves replacement and error semantics, not integration with the real dependency resolver, UIKit, or the app. When reading the repository, follow the active Sources directory and its manifest. When practicing, keep the program small enough that each language effect has an obvious reason.

quiz.question: Why does storing a callback parameter on an object require @escaping?
options: Because it always executes on a background queue.
Because its lifetime can extend beyond the initializing function call.
Because only escaping closures can throw.
quiz.explanation: Escaping is a lifetime annotation. Thread choice, capture strength, throwing behavior, and whether the callback is eventually invoked are separate properties.

quiz.question: A helper exists only in a protocol extension, and a conformer declares the same method. Which is selected through an any-protocol value?
options: The conformer's same-named method in every situation.
The extension-only helper based on the protocol-typed access.
The compiler dynamically adds the method to the protocol.
quiz.explanation: Only declared requirements establish the polymorphic contract. Make the method a protocol requirement when calls through the protocol must dispatch to conformer-specific implementations.

quiz.question: What behavior is lost by try? service.providers() ?? []?
options: The ability to distinguish failed retrieval from successful empty data.
The ability to make arrays immutable.
The ability to use trailing closures.
quiz.explanation: Both outcomes become the same empty array, discarding the offline error needed for retry or a failure presentation.

quiz.question: What does any ProviderServing imply about the underlying service?
options: It must be a class.
Its concrete conforming type is hidden behind the protocol contract.
It is automatically safe to share across actors.
quiz.explanation: An existential can hold a conforming struct or class. It does not change value/reference semantics or add a concurrency safety guarantee.

exercise.brief: Build a fake appointment service. Show data, an empty success, and offline failure through separate callbacks.
steps: Declare AppointmentServing with appointments() throws -> [String]. Declare AppointmentFailure.offline as an Error case.
Give the fake a Result<[String], AppointmentFailure>. Explain what each type inside the angle brackets means.
Add a count helper in a protocol extension. Keep throws so failure is still reported.
Write a consumer taking any AppointmentServing, an onSuccess callback, and an onFailure callback.
Run all three outcomes. Explain whether either callback can outlive this synchronous call and therefore needs @escaping.
acceptance: Nonempty and empty arrays both invoke success exactly once.
Offline invokes failure and never masquerades as a zero-count success.
The extension helper preserves errors.
Callbacks run during the synchronous consumer call and need no @escaping.
No real appointments, requests, or production file edits are used.
exercise.solution:
Result is an enum that holds success or failure. Its type arguments inside angle brackets name the success data and the error type. Calling get() returns the successful value or throws the stored error. This answer is a complete standalone program. Keep its declarations separate from the earlier example.

protocol AppointmentServing {
    func appointments() throws -> [String]
}
enum AppointmentFailure: Error { case offline }

struct FakeAppointments: AppointmentServing {
    let result: Result<[String], AppointmentFailure>
    func appointments() throws -> [String] { try result.get() }
}
extension AppointmentServing {
    func count() throws -> Int { try appointments().count }
}
func loadAppointments(
    using service: any AppointmentServing,
    onSuccess: ([String]) -> Void,
    onFailure: (any Error) -> Void
) {
    do {
        onSuccess(try service.appointments())
    } catch {
        onFailure(error)
    }
}
let outcomes: [Result<[String], AppointmentFailure>] = [
    .success(["Synthetic visit"]),
    .success([]),
    .failure(.offline)
]
for outcome in outcomes {
    loadAppointments(
        using: FakeAppointments(result: outcome),
        onSuccess: { print("Success count:", $0.count) },
        onFailure: { print("Failure:", $0) }
    )
}

The two success lines contain counts 1 and 0. The failure line reports offline. The helper and consumer do not silently substitute defaults. Both callbacks are ordinary nonescaping parameters because no code stores or returns them. If you later put onSuccess in a retained handler, change the parameter annotation and review what it captures; adding escaping alone does not establish correct ownership.

lessons.title: ARC, capture lists, and ownership graphs
lessons.summary: Find who keeps an object alive, then choose strong, weak, or unowned references for that lifetime.
objectives: Explain why an unreachable strong cycle can survive ARC even though a garbage collector can collect it.
Draw the strong and weak links made by a stored callback.
Use a weak capture and explain how guard let temporarily keeps the object alive.
Predict captured values, nested captures, and what unowned promises about lifetime.

sections.title: Ask who still keeps the screen alive
sections.html:
ARC means Automatic Reference Counting. It manages class objects by tracking strong references that keep them alive. On Android, an Activity kept by a singleton listener stays reachable, so the garbage collector cannot release it. Swift adds another question: do surviving objects keep each other alive? Inspect callbacks as you would on Android, then draw those strong links too.

Under JVM garbage collection, a cycle that is unreachable from roots can be collected. Android ART also uses garbage collection, though it is not the same collector implementation as desktop HotSpot. Under Swift ARC, an isolated cycle of strong references can keep its participants alive. Removing the screen's external variable does not remove the internal owning edges.

ARC is automatic, but ownership design remains your responsibility. Values such as structs do not have class identity; nevertheless a struct can contain references whose lifetime ARC manages. Closures can retain captured class objects. These facts connect directly to sessions 001 and 003: a value wrapper is not a deep-copy boundary, and an escaping callback may outlive the function that created it.

We will use synchronous toy screens in standalone Swift. There are no UIKit views, threads, or delayed timers, so the evidence will concern ownership only. The same reasoning is later applied to a production view controller, with its lifecycle and task behavior inspected separately.

sections.title: Draw the loop before choosing a fix
sections.html:
A strong cycle is a loop of references in which each object keeps the next one alive. In this program, screen first keeps the instance alive. The instance stores tapCallback. That closure uses self.name, so it keeps the same instance alive too. Setting screen to nil removes the outside owner. It leaves the two inside links in place. Read the example as a graph before running it.

final class CyclicScreen {
    let name = "Synthetic screen"
    var tapCallback: (() -> Void)?
    func install() {
        tapCallback = { print(self.name) }
    }
    deinit { print("CyclicScreen released") }
}

func inspectCycle() {
    var screen: CyclicScreen? = CyclicScreen()
    screen?.install()
    weak var probe = screen
    screen = nil
    print(probe != nil) // true: stored closure still owns screen
    probe?.tapCallback = nil  // explicitly clean up the intentional cycle
    print(probe == nil) // true
}
inspectCycle()

(() -> Void)? is an optional zero-argument closure. The outer question mark applies to the function value, allowing tapCallback to be absent. deinit runs when the class instance is deallocated; it cannot rescue a cycle that prevents deallocation. Placing tapCallback = nil only inside deinit would therefore be ineffective.

The weak probe observes without owning. Its staying nonnil after external ownership disappears demonstrates a remaining owner. Clearing tapCallback removes the screen-to-closure edge, which releases the closure and its capture. The demonstration deliberately cleans up; a lesson should not leave a leak running merely to prove that leaks exist.

sections.title: Let a saved callback tolerate a missing screen
sections.html:
A weak reference lets you reach an object without keeping it alive. Once the object is released, Swift makes that reference nil. Use it when a callback may survive its screen and should skip work if the screen is gone. Weak references apply to class instances or protocols restricted to classes. They must be optional variables because their targets can disappear.

final class WeakScreen {
    let name = "Synthetic screen"
    var tapCallback: (() -> Void)?
    func install() {
        tapCallback = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else {
                print("Skipped: screen is gone")
                return
            }
            print(self.name)
        }
    }
    deinit { print("WeakScreen released") }
}

func inspectWeakCapture() {
    var screen: WeakScreen? = WeakScreen()
    screen?.install()
    let savedCallback = screen?.tapCallback
    weak var probe = screen
    savedCallback?()
    screen = nil
    print(probe == nil) // true
    savedCallback?()   // safely prints Skipped
}
inspectWeakCapture()

The square brackets introduce the closure's capture list. [weak self] stores a nonowning optional reference; in starts the body. guard let self checks that the object is still present, then creates a strong local reference for its use. That local keeps the object alive while it is needed. It does not turn the saved weak capture into permanent ownership.

SavedCallback owns the closure, but its weak capture does not own the screen. Optional invocation, savedCallback?(), skips the call only if the closure itself is missing. The guard separately handles the closure existing while its screen is gone. These are two different optional checks.

sections.title: Choose a reference from the needed lifetime
sections.html:
A strong reference keeps its target alive. That fits a coordinator owning its child or an operation needing a service until completion. Weak observes an object owned elsewhere and accepts its disappearance. Ordinary nonoptional unowned also avoids keeping the target alive, but later access traps if the target has gone. Choose unowned only when you can prove the target outlives every use.

ReferenceRetains targetTarget ends first
StrongYesIts ownership must end before deallocation
WeakNoReference becomes nil
Unowned, ordinary formNoLater access traps

Unowned optional references also exist, but they do not gain weak's automatic nil behavior. For this beginner sequence, use weak for externally retained callbacks unless you can prove the target outlives every use. Do not execute a crashing unowned demonstration in the exercise.

Making every capture weak can silently drop required work. If a save operation must complete independently of a screen, a service or operation owner may need to retain the necessary dependency. If screen updates should be discarded after dismissal, a weak screen capture may be exactly right. Write the desired lifetime first, then select the reference.

Likewise, a temporary strong reference is not automatically a leak. A retained operation can release everything after completion. Ask what owns the operation, whether completion is guaranteed, and whether cancellation or clearing a callback breaks the path. A graph with a bounded release path deserves different analysis from a permanent cycle.

sections.title: Choose the value a callback remembers
sections.html:
A capture list is the square-bracket list at the start of a closure. It can choose which value the closure remembers as well as how it refers to an object. A closure reading a mutable local can see later edits. An explicit capture initialized from that local remembers its value when the closure is created. This example uses strings, so no class lifetime is involved.

var label = "Before"
let live = { print(label) }
let snapshot = { [label] in print(label) }
label = "After"
live()     // After
snapshot() // Before

[label] captures the current string value under the same local name. You can give the captured value another name, such as [initialLabel = label]. If the captured value is a class reference, capturing it strongly keeps that object; it does not freeze the object's properties or clone it. A snapshot of a reference is still a reference.

Draw nested closures separately. After guard unwraps weak self, the local self is strong. An inner saved closure using that local can keep the object alive. It does not inherit weak behavior from the outer closure. A Task using the same local across a wait also needs a new lifetime check: who keeps that work, and when does it finish or release its captures?

Last use means the final point where the program needs a local value. The compiler may end that value's lifetime after its last use. A deinit print therefore is not a universal promise about release at an exact source line under every optimization setting. Weak probes and deliberate removal of known owners give clearer evidence. Async work also requires inspecting task storage and completion.

sections.title: Follow the real callback owners
sections.html:
An ownership path lists what keeps what alive. Open CancelAppointmentViewController at line 85. It saves a callback on subview.on. The view owns its Actions container at line 21. Actions stores tappedContinue near line 229. Draw controller → view → Actions → callback. The callback uses weak self, so its return link to the controller does not keep that controller alive.

The longer guard let self = self in this source and the shorter guard let self in our example both unwrap the optional into a local binding. Their spelling differs; the ownership purpose is the same. The current project also contains modern and legacy idioms, so learning one concise form does not require rewriting every older form.

In the coordinator at line 64, the outer callback captures self weakly, unwraps it, then creates a Task at line 77 that uses self. That inner closure retains the unwrapped coordinator for its use. This snippet shows retention; it does not, by itself, prove a permanent cycle or establish a cancellation policy. Inspect task storage, completion, and the awaited service before making that diagnosis.

Explicitly list what you can conclude and what remains unknown. You can identify the weak outer edge and strong inner use. You cannot conclude that every request terminates promptly, that dismissal cancels work, or that memory is released immediately afterward. Ownership analysis improves when claims stay tied to inspected evidence.

quiz.question: Why can a cycle that JVM GC collects remain alive under Swift ARC?
options: ARC never releases class instances.
The cycle's strong ownership edges remain even after external ownership is removed.
Swift closures always live until app termination.
quiz.explanation: A tracing collector can recognize a root-unreachable cycle. ARC needs the remaining owning references to be broken; screen and stored closure can retain one another.

quiz.question: Inside a [weak self] closure, what does guard let self establish?
options: A strong local reference for the subsequent work.
A new weak reference that can disappear during each property access.
Automatic cancellation of nested tasks.
quiz.explanation: Successful optional binding retains the instance through the local use. A nested closure can capture this new binding strongly, so its lifetime needs another review.

quiz.question: A saved weak-capturing callback is invoked after the screen is released. What should happen?
options: A forced unwrap is required.
Its optional self is nil, so it follows the chosen absent-owner path.
The saved closure automatically recreates the screen.
quiz.explanation: The callback may still exist independently of its owner. Weak capture allows safe disappearance; its body must deliberately handle that case.

quiz.question: What justifies unowned rather than weak for an escaping callback?
options: The target is usually fast.
A proven lifetime relationship ensuring the target outlives every callback use.
The class has a deinit method.
quiz.explanation: Ordinary unowned access traps after the target is gone. Speed and deinit presence do not establish the required lifetime invariant.

exercise.brief: Show a callback cycle, remove it, and then use a weak callback safely after its screen is released.
steps: Run or recreate inspectCycle. Draw each strong link before and after screen = nil.
Explain why the weak probe still finds the screen. Clear tapCallback explicitly and check that the screen is released.
Write the weak version before looking at the answer. Keep a separate copy of its callback.
Call that saved callback before and after releasing the screen. Record how the output changes.
Predict what unowned would do after release without running a crashing example. Give one case where strong retention is needed.
acceptance: The cyclic demonstration cleans up after itself.
The weak probe becomes nil when strong owners are removed in the repaired version.
The saved callback safely handles missing self.
Both diagrams label ownership, and the explanation separates callback storage from its captured object.
No claim of a production memory fix or app build is made.
exercise.solution:
The loop is screen → instance → tapCallback closure → instance. Each arrow is strong, so each keeps its target alive. Setting screen to nil removes only the first arrow. Clearing the stored callback breaks the loop. Cleanup placed only in deinit cannot help: the loop stops the instance from being released and reaching that method.

The repaired graph is screen → instance → tapCallback closure ⇢ instance, where the last arrow is weak. A saved callback adds an independent strong owner of the closure, not of its weakly referenced screen. With the external screen variable cleared, the weak probe becomes nil; invocation follows the guard's absent-owner branch.

The complete code above provides the worked implementations. Expected observations are true for remaining retention in inspectCycle, true for cleanup afterward, true for release in inspectWeakCapture, and Skipped after invoking the saved callback post-release. Treat deinit output as supporting evidence in this controlled program rather than a timing contract for every optimization level.

For the final ownership choice, consider queued work that must finish even after a view disappears. A dedicated queue may strongly own that operation and its service until completion, then clear its stored work. That is bounded retention if the release path is guaranteed. If the owner also permanently owns the queue and its operation captures the owner, inspect the new cycle. Each added closure deserves its own graph.

lessons.title: Xcode, SwiftPM, and Tuist through a Gradle lens
lessons.summary: Find which files a build uses, what it makes, and which tool and OS settings apply.
objectives: Compare Gradle modules and variants with Xcode targets, schemes, configurations, and packages, and state where the comparison breaks.
Tell the compiler version, tools version, language mode, SDK, and oldest supported OS apart.
Find active source files and dependencies in the Tuist manifests.
Choose a Swift file, swift test, or an Xcode destination based on the code's imports.

sections.title: Find the build that actually uses your file
sections.html:
A build graph is the map of components and the other components they need. You have seen Android builds fail because a file belongs to the wrong module, a variant has different dependencies, or the JDK does not fit the plugin. iOS has similar problems spread across several tools. Start by finding which chosen target compiles your file. A file being present on disk does not mean this build uses it.

Xcode is Apple's development app. Its toolchain is the collection of compilers, SDKs, simulators, and build tools it uses. Swift Package Manager, called SwiftPM or SPM, reads package declarations for targets, dependencies, and products. Tuist reads Swift manifests to generate Xcode projects. They work together and do different jobs. Knowing one command does not make the other tools interchangeable.

Start with one question: what artifact and destination am I asking the tools to build? A pure Swift model can run as a standalone program or a host-compatible package. A file importing UIKit needs an Apple platform target with the relevant SDK. A unit test bundle needs its test target and runner. Successfully running a model snippet does not imply that an iOS app, signing, or integration was validated.

sections.title: Name the component, settings, and action plan
sections.html:
A target describes one buildable component: its files, dependencies, settings, and output. A scheme plans actions such as building, running, and testing those targets. A configuration, such as Debug, supplies build settings. A destination chooses a device, simulator, or supported host. These are separate choices. The table compares them with Android ideas; each comparison has a limit.

Android ideaClosest iOS conceptBoundary
Gradle moduleTarget or package targetA package may contain several targets and products
Build type/flavor combinationConfiguration plus target and scheme choicesA scheme is an action plan, not a flavor
AAR/JAR or APK artifactLibrary product, framework, app, or test bundleArtifact type and linking rules differ
settings.gradle project graphWorkspace and dependency graphA workspace groups projects rather than compiling one module
Gradle tasksBuild, run, test, archive actionsActions select targets, configuration, and destination

A workspace can contain multiple projects and their dependencies. A project can contain an app, frameworks, unit tests, UI tests, and extensions. A SwiftPM product exposes one or more package targets as a library or executable to downstream clients. Import usually names a module, not necessarily a package or product. Do not assume a directory's name is the import name without checking its target.

An app's bundle identifier distinguishes its installed identity; it is not the same concept as a Swift module name. An app extension is its own target with separate capabilities and packaging, rather than a source set inside the app. We will revisit signing later; here the purpose is to locate the correct graph node.

sections.title: Keep the five version questions separate
sections.html:
A compiler translates source code and checks language rules. Run xcrun swift --version to see the selected Swift compiler. xcodebuild -version reports the Xcode tool distribution. Earlier course authoring checks reported Apple Swift 6.4 and Xcode 27.1. Those observations describe that environment. Check your own selection. They are not minimum course requirements and do not tell you every client target's Swift language mode.

The // swift-tools-version: line states the minimum package tools version. It also chooses the PackageDescription APIs the manifest may use and influences default language settings. It does not name the installed compiler or the oldest supported iOS version. Check explicit package or target language settings too before deciding how source is checked.

The language mode chooses compatibility and checking rules, including Swift 6's stronger concurrency checks. A newer compiler can use an older mode. The SDK supplies platform APIs at compile time. The deployment target names the oldest OS the output supports. An API may exist in the SDK and still be unavailable on that older runtime. Check availability separately from whether the import compiles.

In this checkout, ZDAppointments Package.swift declares tools 5.9 and iOS 17. ZDHome declares tools 6.1 and iOS 17, and its Project.swift explicitly sets SWIFT_VERSION to 6. The production app settings helper carries 5.0. This is a mixed graph. Never diagnose a Swift 6 concurrency error by reading only the tools line of an unrelated package.

sections.title: Read one small package first
sections.html:
A manifest is a file that describes a package to its build tool. This example describes an isolated model library that can run on the host computer. It needs no UIKit, remote package, app identifier, or signing setup. Use it in your own scratch directory. Reading this small map first makes the larger client manifests easier to follow.

// swift-tools-version: 5.9
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "FoundationLab",
    products: [
        .library(name: "FoundationLab", targets: ["FoundationLab"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "FoundationLab"),
        .testTarget(
            name: "FoundationLabTests",
            dependencies: ["FoundationLab"]
        )
    ]
)

The library product exports FoundationLab's target. The test target depends on that target; putting a test file beside production sources would not automatically make it a discovered test. By convention, source lives under Sources/FoundationLab and tests under Tests/FoundationLabTests. A custom target path can override those conventions, so inspect before assuming.

import PackageDescription makes manifest APIs available; it is not an import your model needs at runtime. For an iOS package, platforms can declare a minimum iOS version, but that does not make UIKit buildable through a default macOS swift test invocation. The selected build environment still matters.

Dependencies can name local packages, version ranges, exact versions, or revisions. A resolved dependency file records selected versions; it serves a role related to lockfiles, not to source membership. Keep manifest intent and resolved selections conceptually separate. Credentials or network failure during resolution should not be mistaken for a syntax failure in your new model.

sections.title: Find the active sources in this checkout
sections.html:
Source membership says which files a target compiles. Open ZDAppointments Project.swift. The cancellation target at line 44 builds an iOS static framework: a library linked into its caller. Its oldest supported iOS version is 17.0. The pattern Sources/ZDAppointmentsCancellation/**/*.swift at line 49 selects its source files. The separate test target at line 101 has its own file pattern and depends on this library.

The nearby Package.swift lists matching targets for the retained SwiftPM route. Workspace.swift names Zocdoc-Tuist and lists its app entry projects; their dependencies bring more projects into the build map. Current manifests use Project.swift for local projects. Tuist/Package.swift keeps remote dependencies and special settings. An old migration comment is not enough to tell which route builds a local feature now.

Tuist configuration and project generation are different from compiling app code. The repository pins Tuist 4.203.4 in mise.toml. Use the pinned workflow rather than globally installing a different version for this exercise. Generated project files can be regenerated from the manifests; a hand edit may disappear at the next generation. Check ownership before changing a build setting.

Sources also need target dependencies for their imports. If a file exists but its module cannot be imported, inspect target membership, product exposure, dependency edges, and destination before clearing caches. Cache deletion is not a substitute for explaining the graph.

sections.title: Choose a check that fits the code
sections.html:
A host check runs on your development computer. A standalone Swift file is enough for a language-only experiment. A pure model package can use swift test. UIKit code needs a suitable Apple SDK and iOS target. For simulator work or app-hosted tests, choose the Xcode workspace, scheme, and destination. Running a macOS script cannot verify a UIKit test.

xcrun swift --version
xcodebuild -version
# From your own host-compatible FoundationLab package:
swift test
# Replace the placeholder with an existing inspected workspace:
xcodebuild -list -workspace /path/to/Existing.xcworkspace

The first two commands inspect tool selection. The final command lists workspace structure; it does not build or prove dependencies can resolve. The placeholder is intentionally not a discovered path in this workspace. Read the available schemes and match them to manifests before selecting one for a build.

When a build fails, classify the first actionable diagnostic: parsing/type checking, module resolution, linking, destination/SDK, signing, or test discovery. Search upward from the failing target rather than treating every failure as an Xcode problem. Record the chosen workspace, target, scheme, configuration, destination, and compiler as evidence.

There is no need to regenerate the shared app or modify its setup to learn today's model. The next session uses an isolated FoundationLab package. That scope gives fast feedback on value semantics and contracts while keeping full app dependencies out of the language exercise.

lessons.title: Model and testing lab: a tiny search core
lessons.summary: Build a small Swift search model and use controlled tests to prove its important rules.
objectives: Build a value draft, a state enum, a service protocol, and a synchronous loading function.
Test user-facing behavior rather than the number or order of code branches.
Write Swift Testing checks and recognize the matching XCTest style.
Say what model tests on the host prove and what still needs app testing.

sections.title: Keep the first lab small enough to explain
sections.html:
A fake is a substitute whose answers you control. Like a Kotlin reducer test with a fake repository, this lab uses a draft, a set of states, a service promise, and one loading function. The function is synchronous: it finishes within the call. There is no screen, network, or database. This small scope helps you tell a language mistake from a broken product rule or a setup problem.

The product rules are concrete. A draft edit must not mutate the original. An absent procedure remains absent rather than becoming a sentinel ID. A missing specialty requires a choice. A successful query with no results remains successful. An offline service failure produces a retry state. A successful nonempty response preserves its names.

Use synthetic names and identifiers throughout. The production cancellation feature supplies examples of model and test organization; we are not importing its data or claiming to reproduce its business rules. Reading the worked solution is useful reference material, but it does not pre-complete your exercise. Save predictions first and compare them with the tests you run.

Plan about twenty minutes for modeling, twenty for test construction, twenty for implementation, and the remaining time for explaining failures and documenting limits. The lab can also be completed on paper with predicted test outcomes if a compatible toolchain is unavailable.

sections.title: Give source and tests their own folders
sections.html:
A test target is the component that holds and runs your checks. In a scratch directory, use Sources/FoundationLab for the library and Tests/FoundationLabTests for tests. The manifest below needs a Swift 6.0-or-newer toolchain for this Swift Testing lab. Earlier authoring checks used Swift 6.4. That is a lab environment observation, not a change to the client's mixed build settings.

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "FoundationLab",
    products: [
        .library(name: "FoundationLab", targets: ["FoundationLab"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "FoundationLab"),
        .testTarget(
            name: "FoundationLabTests",
            dependencies: ["FoundationLab"]
        )
    ]
)

The manifest has no remote dependency. Its library can compile on the host because we use only ordinary Swift types. Put the model and load function under the library target, and put test imports and fakes under the test target. swift test is run from this scratch package, not from the full client root.

import Testing imports the test framework. FoundationLab is the application module. @testable import FoundationLab lets tests use its internal declarations when built with testing enabled. It does not open private declarations or turn internal types into public API. The test target needs both a dependency on FoundationLab and the import. Those solve separate setup requirements.

sections.title: Write the model rules before the code
sections.html:
An invariant is a rule the model must keep true. SearchDraft is a struct with optional Int64 identifiers and a query string. Its calculated displayQuery says All providers only when query is empty. It leaves the stored query alone. Write the ID rules separately: no procedure is allowed, but no specialty blocks a search. A display fallback must not silently replace missing data in the model.

LabSearchState names idle, loading, loaded names, and failed message. A future UI may need all four. This synchronous function returns a final loaded or failed value. It does not publish a loading step while it runs. An async owner would manage those transitions later. Do not add a fake temporary return state just to use every enum case.

The protocol has one operation: search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String]. The external label for reads naturally at the call; draft is the local parameter name. Passing the draft by value makes the service boundary explicit. It does not stop a conforming class from managing its own internal state.

Make the fake configurable with Result. A successful empty array and an offline error then require different fixture constructors. This is more honest than a fake with one Boolean whose meaning changes between tests. Keep the fake in the test target unless it serves a real runtime purpose. Avoid designing a reusable mocking framework before the first behavior is proven.

sections.title: Turn service outcomes into clear states
sections.html:
A boundary is where one part of the program hands work or data to another. Here load calls a service and turns its answer into a screen state. Try writing it first, then compare it with the library source below. These declarations are internal, so this package's tests can use them with a testable import. No Foundation or UI import is needed.

struct SearchDraft: Equatable {
    var specialtyID: Int64?
    var procedureID: Int64?
    var query: String

    var displayQuery: String {
        query.isEmpty ? "All providers" : query
    }
}

enum LabSearchState: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loading
    case loaded(providers: [String])
    case failed(message: String)
}

enum LabSearchError: Error { case offline }

protocol LabProviderServing {
    func search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String]
}

func load(
    draft: SearchDraft,
    service: any LabProviderServing
) -> LabSearchState {
    guard draft.specialtyID != nil else {
        return .failed(message: "Choose a specialty")
    }
    do {
        return .loaded(providers: try service.search(for: draft))
    } catch LabSearchError.offline {
        return .failed(message: "Offline: retry")
    } catch {
        return .failed(message: "Unable to search")
    }
}

The guard checks the specialty requirement before calling the service. It checks absence rather than rejecting a numeric sentinel. The do block produces loaded even when the returned array is empty. The first catch maps the known offline case to retry guidance; the final catch supplies a generic unexpected-failure message.

This small boundary intentionally turns service errors into presentation states. In production you might retain a typed failure, expose a retry policy, or report an error through an observability boundary. A generic message should not be your only diagnostic evidence in a real app. Here, synchronous deterministic mapping isolates the distinction we want to learn.

Neither this function nor the protocol implements thread safety, request cancellation, input trimming, localization, caching, or result ordering. Those are future requirements. A model test is most useful when it makes its scope explicit instead of implying that a passing assertion covers unimplemented concerns.

sections.title: Read the test and its assertion
sections.html:
An assertion checks a claim about the result. Swift Testing finds functions marked @Test. #expect checks a condition and records useful details when it fails. Both are supplied by the Testing module. A suite groups tests; a parameterized test repeats a check with different inputs. The active cancellation tests already use these features.

XCTest is also widely used, including for UI automation and older tests. An XCTest unit test conventionally subclasses XCTestCase and defines methods beginning with test; assertions such as XCTAssertEqual express expectations. This optional alternative belongs in a test target that has the lab module available:

import XCTest
@testable import FoundationLab

final class SearchDraftXCTests: XCTestCase {
    func testDisplayQueryForEmptyInput() {
        let draft = SearchDraft(
            specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: ""
        )
        XCTAssertEqual(draft.displayQuery, "All providers")
    }
}

Choose the framework already used by the target and the behavior you need. Do not mix XCTest assertion APIs inside a Swift Testing test and assume identical failure reporting. The two frameworks can coexist in a test target, but that is not a reason to duplicate every assertion.

Keep each test's fixtures local. Swift Testing can execute tests in parallel, so shared mutable globals turn a simple value-model test into an order-dependent exercise. Avoid sleeps: the core is synchronous and needs none. A fake gives controlled results directly.

sections.title: Make a failing test explain a broken rule
sections.html:
A fixture is a small known input prepared for a test. The tests below use fixtures to check separate edits, display fallbacks, empty success, offline failure, missing specialty, and preserved names. Put them in Tests/FoundationLabTests. They check the result of the library call. They do not require a particular number of branches inside your implementation.

import Testing
@testable import FoundationLab

struct FakeLabService: LabProviderServing {
    let result: Result<[String], LabSearchError>
    func search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String] {
        try result.get()
    }
}

@Test func editingPreservesOriginal() {
    let original = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: ""
    )
    var edited = original
    edited.specialtyID = 20
    #expect(original.specialtyID == 10)
    #expect(edited.specialtyID == 20)
    #expect(original.procedureID == nil)
    #expect(original.displayQuery == "All providers")
}

@Test func successfulEmptyAndFailureRemainDistinct() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: "Ada"
    )
    let empty = load(
        draft: draft, service: FakeLabService(result: .success([]))
    )
    let offline = load(
        draft: draft, service: FakeLabService(result: .failure(.offline))
    )
    #expect(empty == .loaded(providers: []))
    #expect(offline == .failed(message: "Offline: retry"))
    #expect(empty != offline)
}

@Test func missingSpecialtyRequiresAChoice() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: nil, procedureID: nil, query: ""
    )
    let state = load(
        draft: draft,
        service: FakeLabService(result: .success(["Dr. Ada"]))
    )
    #expect(state == .failed(message: "Choose a specialty"))
}

@Test func nonemptySuccessKeepsNames() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: "Ada"
    )
    let state = load(
        draft: draft,
        service: FakeLabService(result: .success(["Dr. Ada"]))
    )
    #expect(state == .loaded(providers: ["Dr. Ada"]))
}

The first test would catch accidental reference semantics in a mutable model. The second would catch replacing errors with empty arrays. The third would catch omission of the validation rule, and the fourth protects nonempty success. A failure should lead to an explanation of which product fact was violated, not simply a change to the expected string until everything turns green.

As a diagnostic exercise, temporarily replace the do/catch implementation with .loaded(providers: (try? service.search(for: draft)) ?? []). Predict which assertion fails before running. Restore the explicit error mapping afterward. This controlled mutation shows that the failure-distinction test protects something real.

Open the active booking-prompt tests at their repository anchor. They use descriptive Test labels, locally constructed responses, and parameterized inputs for business variants. Copy the discipline of controlled fixtures and named behavior, not the domain-specific cancellation codes. Their inclusion is confirmed by the cancellation test source glob.

quiz.explanation: The test protects a product distinction at the boundary. Importing or measuring code cannot show that retry information survived.

options: Access to internal declarations when built for testing, without making all private details public.

quiz.question: Why keep fake configuration and fixtures local to each Swift Testing test?
options: Because structs cannot be global.
Because parallel tests should not interfere through shared mutable state.
Because Swift Testing prohibits all reusable helpers.
quiz.explanation: Parallel execution can expose shared mutable fixture races and order dependence. Reusable pure helpers are fine; local ownership keeps each case deterministic.

options: The iOS app is signed, accessible, and ready to release.
The tested pure model behaviors work in this host-compatible package.

quiz.explanation: Scope matters. The lab checks its own core and fixtures; app integration, platforms, UI, and networking still require their respective verification.

The model and Swift Testing blocks above are the worked answer. In your scratch package, run swift test beside Package.swift. The four named Swift Testing tests should pass for the shown implementation. Adding the optional XCTest example adds another test.
