sections.title: Recall first, then check your reasoning
sections.html:
Retrieval practice means recalling a rule before looking it up. As an experienced Android engineer, you may understand Swift while reading, then reach for Kotlin rules under pressure. Today you predict small programs, explain mistakes, and follow one feature from model to callback to build target. The aim is to reason with changed inputs. Remembering the example's printed words alone is not enough.

Close the earlier lesson text for the first pass. Write answers with confidence marks: certain, tentative, or guessing. Then check the worked explanations and run the isolated snippets if you have the toolchain. When a prediction changes, write the assumption that misled you. For example, replacing val with let is easy; remembering that a struct bound to let cannot mutate a stored field is a different skill.

Use three columns in your notes: observation, language rule, and product consequence. An array is empty is an observation; successful data is not an error is a domain distinction; show no matches rather than retry is a product consequence. This format prevents correct-looking syntax from substituting for a correct explanation.

Keep unfinished exercises pending. Instructor examples and your own practice remain separate evidence.

sections.title: Predict separate fields and shared objects
sections.html:
Aliasing means two references reach the same object. Before running this standalone program, predict its three printed values. Say which struct fields belong to separate values and which field still points to one shared Notes object. Then check whether the empty query uses the fallback. Finally, decide whether changing first.query would compile and name the rule behind your answer.

final class ReviewNotes { var text = "Initial" }
struct ReviewDraft {
    var query: String
    var specialtyID: Int64?
    let notes: ReviewNotes
}

let first = ReviewDraft(
    query: "", specialtyID: nil, notes: ReviewNotes()
)
var edited = first
edited.query = "Ada"
edited.notes.text = "Shared"

Worked prediction — open after answering

The outputs are true, Shared, and a blank line. The outer struct values have independent query fields, but both contain the same Notes reference. A present empty string is not nil, so nil coalescing preserves it. Now retrieve the syntax distinctions without checking session 001. What external label is used for func subtitle(for draft: ReviewDraft)? Why might a wire identifier use Int64 rather than Int? What extra contract does Hashable provide beyond Equatable? Does String.count mean the same thing as Kotlin String.length for every Unicode input?

Explain each answer with a concrete consequence. Argument labels affect call sites; integer width affects data contracts; hashing affects collections rather than identity; text representation affects length limits. Facts become useful when you can name the bug they prevent.

sections.title: Rebuild the states from the product rules
sections.html:
An associated-value enum names choices and gives each choice the data it needs. On a blank page, write idle, loading, loaded names, and failed message. Write a title function without default. Show one title for successful empty results and another for offline failure. Add a pretend offline case. Identify which switches the compiler should ask you to revisit.

Worked reasoning — open after drafting

An associated-value enum stores names only in loaded and an error description only in failed. An exhaustive switch exposes missing handling when a new local case is introduced. Empty loaded results should express no matches; idle should express a search not yet begun; failure should retain enough meaning to offer recovery. The enum controls representable combinations, while a separate owner still controls valid transitions.

For a second retrieval task, compare case failed(message: String) with enum Reason: String. Which data varies per instance? What happens when a raw-value initializer receives a newly introduced server string? Do not answer by saying both are enums; describe the different boundary behavior.

A good answer notes that associated data varies for each construction and a raw value is fixed for each case. Unknown raw input yields nil, requiring a compatibility decision. Neither form automatically validates message contents or becomes Codable just because it has strings.

Finally, consider a requirement to preserve old results while loading new ones. Our simple four-state model cannot express that directly. You could add a loading payload, nest a request status inside a content model, or define another appropriate state. Identify the product rule first. Retrieval includes knowing when a previously useful model has reached its limit.

sections.title: Check the promise and keep the error
sections.html:
An existential lets a caller use a value through a protocol without naming its concrete type. Explain a consumer taking any ProviderServing. Its service could be a struct or a class. Say why a synchronous fake can replace the real service. Check the method name, labels, types, and effects. Then say what the callers must change if the protocol becomes async.

Next, audit the expression (try? service.providers()) ?? []. It is valid Swift, so a compiler will not reject the product mistake. Name two originally distinct outcomes and the UI affordance lost after the transformation. Then rewrite the boundary with do/catch or a typed result so that empty success and failure remain distinct.

Worked contract and failure explanation

A conformer satisfies the required operation's name, labels, types, and effects. The existential hides the concrete type, which can be a value or reference. Ordinary throws requires explicit try at the call. Async adds suspension to the contract rather than merely decorating an implementation. The optional fallback erases the error and makes offline look like zero matches, losing retry meaning.

Recall how Swift picks an extension method. If the method exists only in a protocol extension, a protocol-typed value uses that helper even when its concrete type has a same-named method. If conformer-specific behavior is promised to callers, declare the method as a protocol requirement. An extension may still supply its default. This distinction can explain why a fake and real implementation appear to take different paths.

Finally, define escaping without mentioning threads. A stored plain closure parameter must be marked escaping because it can outlive the call. That annotation does not make it weak, Sendable, asynchronous, or guaranteed to run. Those are separate reviews.

sections.title: Draw which callback keeps which owner alive
sections.html:
A stored callback remains reachable through the object that holds it. Draw an owner holding a callback that strongly captures that owner. Erase the outside variable. Mark the links still present. Could deinit break this loop? Now change the capture to weak. Explain what happens when you save the callback elsewhere, release its owner, and call it again.

Worked ownership explanation

The owner-to-callback and callback-to-owner strong edges keep the cycle alive. Deinit cannot remove a loop that prevents deallocation. Weak capture removes the callback's owning edge; a saved callback can remain alive while its captured owner becomes nil. Its body needs a deliberate absent-owner path. Optional callback invocation and optional owner unwrapping solve different absence cases.

For a harder question, the weak callback performs guard let self and creates another stored closure using self. Label the inner capture. Explain why the outer capture policy does not automatically apply to the nested closure. If the stored work is cleared after execution, what distinguishes temporary retention from an unbounded leak?

The guard introduces a strong local owner. The inner closure can retain that binding until its own lifetime ends. You must inspect who stores the inner work and when it releases it. A guaranteed release path can make retention appropriate; a new cycle or a never-completing operation can keep resources alive unexpectedly.

Choose unowned only from a proven lifetime relationship. Do not propose it merely because a callback is normally fast. Also separate memory lifetime from lifecycle policy: a callback that safely finds a screen alive may still be semantically wrong to update after dismissal. Ownership safety does not decide cancellation or UI validity.

sections.title: Find which build setting answers the question
sections.html:
A language mode selects the language rules used to check a target's source. Suppose the machine has Swift 6.4, ZDAppointments declares tools 5.9 and minimum iOS 17, and another target sets SWIFT_VERSION to 6. Explain why these can all be true. Find the failing target's effective settings. A neighboring target's mode does not answer what this target uses.

The installed compiler, manifest tools requirement, source language mode, and deployment target are separate. Effective build settings for the chosen target and route settle the mode; the newest compiler version alone does not. An SDK can contain APIs unavailable on the minimum supported runtime, so availability also requires explicit reasoning.

Classify three failures: a type does not conform to a protocol; a module cannot be imported; and a test compiles but never runs. The first suggests signature or requirement checking. The second suggests dependency, product exposure, platform, or source membership. The third suggests discovery conventions, test target inclusion, or the scheme's test action. These categories tell you what to inspect next.

Recall five build names in plain words. A target is the component being built. A configuration holds settings. A scheme plans actions with targets. A destination selects a platform or runtime. A workspace groups projects. Project.swift is Swift code describing that build map, not code executing inside the finished app.

For the pure model lab, host swift test is appropriate. For a UIKit test, a suitable iOS destination is needed. A source-only type check, a passing package test, and a successful simulator app build are different evidence. Write the exact verification scope beside each claim.

sections.title: Follow six stops in the active feature
sections.html:
A source trace follows one behavior through the files that implement it. Use the repository links without changing source. Start with the question model's optional subtitle. Follow its calculated NavigationState value and the switch that reads question data. Find the saved submission closure and escaping initializer. Then trace the weak controller callback, the coordinator's nested Task, and the source and test file patterns in Project.swift.

Record an observed line and a justified conclusion at each stop. A source glob proves membership, not successful compilation. Weak capture proves a nonowning edge, not cancellation. The booking-prompt tests connect Testing macros and locally constructed fixtures to business variants; your host-only lab does not replace their platform integration.

Readiness means explaining this chain and implementing a changed example independently. Choose focused practice from your weak spots: three assignment predictions, an added enum case, two error fixtures, or one ownership graph. Revisit it in two days and a week with changed inputs so that you retrieve the rule rather than memorize output.

exercise.solution:
The standalone answer below stores a weak callback because another owner may keep refresh after the screen owner has gone. The fake is a struct with a controlled answer. The owner is a class because this exercise checks reference lifetime. Draft your own version first, then use this program to check your reasoning.

enum ReviewOutcome: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loaded([String])
    case failed(String)
}
enum ReviewFailure: Error { case offline }
protocol ReviewServing {
    func names() throws -> [String]
}
struct ReviewFake: ReviewServing {
    let result: Result<[String], ReviewFailure>
    func names() throws -> [String] { try result.get() }
}
final class ReviewOwner {
    var state: ReviewOutcome = .idle
    var refreshCallback: (() -> Void)?
    let service: any ReviewServing

    init(service: any ReviewServing) {
        self.service = service
        refreshCallback = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            do {
                self.state = .loaded(try self.service.names())
            } catch {
                self.state = .failed("Retry")
            }
        }
    }
}
func summary(of state: ReviewOutcome) -> String {
    switch state {
    case .idle: return "Start"
    case let .loaded(names):
        return names.isEmpty ? "No matches" : "\(names.count) providers"
    case let .failed(message): return message
    }
}
func inspectReviewOwner() {
    var owner: ReviewOwner? = ReviewOwner(
        service: ReviewFake(result: .success([]))
    )
    let saved = owner?.refreshCallback
    weak var probe = owner
    saved?()
    if let state = owner?.state {
        print(summary(of: state)) // No matches
    }
    owner = nil
    print(probe == nil) // true
    saved?()            // missing owner: safely returns
}
inspectReviewOwner()
let offlineOwner = ReviewOwner(
    service: ReviewFake(result: .failure(.offline))
)
offlineOwner.refreshCallback?()
print(summary(of: offlineOwner.state)) // Retry

The controlled output is No matches, true, and Retry. The saved callback survives but its weak owner becomes nil, so the guard returns. The outcome enum preserves successful empty results and failure as different cases. Catching all errors as Retry is a scoped simplification; a production boundary may preserve typed causes.

The initializer stores a newly constructed closure rather than accepting a closure parameter, so there is no parameter to mark escaping. The property's function type does not take an escaping attribute. If a future initializer accepts the stored callback from a caller, that plain closure parameter needs escaping and a fresh ownership review.

Complete your written audit by contrasting this pure program with the active UIKit coordinator. Source and test membership are verified through its Project.swift; the program itself does not verify navigation, task cancellation, localization, signing, or simulator behavior. Choose your next two retrieval tasks from the explanations you had to change, not from the ones that already felt comfortable.

simple.story: Omar practises a route home by drawing it before looking at the map. He marks the bridge, the turning, and the bus stop. On the next attempt, the bus stop has moved. If he memorized only yesterday's turns, he gets lost. If he understands which roads connect, he can redraw the route. He compares his drawing with the map and writes down the wrong assumption. He also separates what he checked on the map from the roads he actually walked. Both notes are useful, but they prove different things.
